slides.text: For five lonely winters on the gale-lashed cliffs of the Isle of Skye, Callum had manned the maritime distress receiver, listening through headphones to static and storm reports from North Sea trawlers. Then, in the dead of January, a bootleg signal slipped between the commercial frequencies: a woman's low, melodic voice reading Neruda poetry and playing scratched vinyl records of Chet Baker. Her transmitter was weak, broadcasting somewhere from the outer hebrides on a pirate frequency of 104.3.

Every night at 2:00 AM, Callum tuned in, keeping his radio mic keyed open just enough so the stranger could hear his kettle whistling and the rain beating against his watchtower window. She never said her name, but she began dedicating songs 'to the listener on the crags who drinks Earl Grey at three in the morning.' For eight months, across seventy miles of black Atlantic water, they built an unspoken home out of copper wire and brass dials.

One November evening, a catastrophic squall knocked out the mainland power grid, silencing the radio bands. Callum stood on his balcony in the pitch black, heartbroken, staring out into the tempestuous sea. Then, three miles across the sound, through the driving sleet, a light began to blink from an old stone cottage. Three short flashes, three long, three short—Morse code for 'I am here.' Callum grabbed his lantern and flashed back into the dark: 'And I am coming.'
